narrative:
Your application was denied because the model assessing your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt predicts an 80.5 percent chance of failure. This is a high-risk outcome, and the university determined that admitting you would likely lead to an unsuccessful result.

The single strongest factor working against you was your class standing in your third year of undergraduate study. You ranked in the bottom decile—a rank of one out of ten—whereas accepted students typically rank near the middle, around sixth. This poor relative performance in your most recent year was the most powerful signal that you might struggle with the rigors of legal education.

Your first-year class ranking also pushed strongly toward a failure prediction, though it was less influential than your third-year standing. Again, being in the bottom decile, compared to the average accepted student’s middle-tier ranking, indicates a pattern of academic difficulty that the model weighed heavily.

Interestingly, your undergraduate GPA worked in your favor, though not enough to overcome the two ranking factors. At 2.80, your GPA is below the average of 3.23 among accepted students, yet it still nudged the prediction toward passing. This suggests that, despite your low class positions, your absolute grades provided some counterbalancing evidence of capability.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing in your final year. Enroll in demanding courses, seek tutoring, and develop stronger study habits to climb out of the bottom decile. Retaking the LSAT to exceed the current average, and addressing any gaps in your preparation, can also strengthen a future application.
